outline.description: State the educational goals for a clinical reference on complement-mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome (CM-HUS), especially when triggered by infection and complicated by sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and thrombotic microangiopathy.
key_points: Recognize the clinical triad of thrombotic microangiopathy: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.
Differentiate CM-HUS from other thrombotic microangiopathies, especially thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, Shiga toxin-associated HUS, and sepsis-associated DIC.
Explain the role of alternative complement pathway dysregulation in CM-HUS and how infection can act as a trigger.

Describe the diagnostic workup for suspected CM-HUS, including hemolysis studies, peripheral smear, ADAMTS13 testing, stool testing for Shiga toxin, complement studies, and kidney biopsy when indicated.
Review the indications, timing, and precautions for complement inhibition with eculizumab, including vaccination and antimicrobial prophylaxis.
Summarize prognosis, relapse considerations, and the role of genetic and functional complement testing in long-term management.

outline.description: Introduce CM-HUS as a complement-driven thrombotic microangiopathy and frame it as a diagnosis of exclusion that may be masked by sepsis-related coagulopathy. Emphasize the relevance of infection-triggered disease in adults, including rare zoonotic triggers such as Capnocytophaga canimorsus.
key_points: CM-HUS is a form of thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulated complement activation, historically termed atypical HUS.
Typical manifestations include MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and renal injury, but presentation can overlap with sepsis, DIC, and multiorgan failure.
Infection is a common trigger for CM-HUS, even in patients without identified inherited complement abnormalities.
C. canimorsus is a rare but important infectious trigger, particularly after dog or cat exposure.
Normal screening complement levels do not exclude CM-HUS.
Early recognition matters because delayed complement blockade is associated with worse renal recovery.

outline.description: Detail the causes and triggers of CM-HUS, distinguishing inherited complement dysregulation, acquired complement abnormalities, and trigger-induced disease. Include infectious triggers and the specific relevance of Capnocytophaga canimorsus.
key_points: Underlying etiologies include genetic variants affecting complement regulators or activators, such as factor H, factor I, factor B, and membrane cofactor protein/CD46.
Acquired causes include autoantibodies, particularly anti-factor H antibodies.
Many patients present only after a triggering event despite incomplete penetrance of complement abnormalities.
Common triggers include infections, pregnancy, autoimmune disease, and certain medications.
CM-HUS may occur without demonstrable pathogenic variants on genetic testing.
C. canimorsus infection can serve as an infectious trigger of CM-HUS following dog bite, scratch, or close animal contact.
The infectious trigger may dominate the early presentation and obscure later emergence of complement-mediated TMA.

outline.description: Summarize the epidemiologic features of CM-HUS without introducing unsupported prevalence figures. Note the rarity of infection-triggered CM-HUS from Capnocytophaga and the adult presentation illustrated by the case.
key_points: CM-HUS is an uncommon cause of thrombotic microangiopathy in adults and children.
Adult cases often require careful distinction from TTP, STEC-HUS, severe hypertension, drug-induced TMA, and sepsis-related TMA.
Infection-triggered CM-HUS is recognized, but specific pathogens vary and unusual organisms may be underrecognized.
C. canimorsus is an uncommon human pathogen acquired from dogs or cats and can cause severe invasive disease.
Capnocytophaga-associated CM-HUS appears to be rare, with only limited case literature.
CM-HUS can occur in immunocompetent adults as well as in patients with traditional infection risk factors.

outline.description: Explain how dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway leads to endothelial injury, platelet consumption, hemolysis, and renal thrombotic microangiopathy. Incorporate the interaction between infection, complement activation, and microvascular thrombosis.
key_points: CM-HUS results from uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway on host endothelial surfaces.
Complement-mediated endothelial injury promotes platelet activation, fibrin deposition, and microvascular thrombosis.
Red blood cells are mechanically fragmented in the microcirculation, causing schistocytosis and MAHA.
Platelet consumption leads to thrombocytopenia, and renal microvascular injury causes AKI, sometimes progressing to anuria and dialysis dependence.
Kidney pathology may show thrombotic microangiopathy with fibrin thrombi, ischemic glomerular changes, and associated acute tubular injury.
Infections may trigger complement activation sufficient to precipitate disease in susceptible individuals or, less commonly, in patients without identified complement mutations.
C. canimorsus creates a biologic paradox: complement contributes to host defense against the organism, yet infection-triggered complement activation may also precipitate endothelial injury and TMA.
Normal C3 and C4 levels do not rule out pathogenic complement dysregulation in CM-HUS.

outline.description: Describe the spectrum of presentation, including the classic TMA features and the way CM-HUS may evolve during or after sepsis. Highlight clues from history, timing, and physical examination that should raise suspicion for superimposed CM-HUS.
key_points: Patients may present with fatigue, pallor, jaundice, reduced urine output, edema, hypertension, or overt AKI.
The classic syndrome includes MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury, but extrarenal manifestations may occur.
Early presentation may be dominated by a triggering illness, especially infection or sepsis.
In infection-associated cases, persistent or new hemolysis and thrombocytopenia after initial sepsis improvement should prompt evaluation for TMA.
History should assess antecedent diarrheal illness, recent infection, animal bite or exposure, pregnancy, autoimmune disease, medications, family history of TMA, and prior similar episodes.
Physical examination may reveal volume overload, purpura or ecchymoses, ischemic digits, neurologic symptoms, and signs of organ dysfunction.
CM-HUS can present after apparent improvement in DIC or sepsis, creating a biphasic clinical course.
Absence of diarrhea does not exclude HUS broadly, but should shift attention away from STEC-HUS when supported by negative microbiology.

outline.description: Outline a practical diagnostic approach to suspected CM-HUS in adults, especially when sepsis or DIC complicates the presentation. Emphasize exclusion of TTP and STEC-HUS, confirmation of hemolysis, and supportive renal pathology when available.
key_points: Initial evaluation should include CBC with platelet count, creatinine, BUN, urinalysis, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, reticulocyte count, coagulation studies, and peripheral blood smear.
Schistocytes on smear support MAHA and raise concern for TMA.
Assess for hemolysis even if initial markers are equivocal, particularly in the setting of recent transfusion, inflammation, or evolving disease.
ADAMTS13 activity is essential to exclude TTP; severe deficiency below 10% strongly supports TTP.
A clinical scoring tool such as PLASMIC may help estimate pretest probability of TTP while awaiting ADAMTS13 results.
Shiga toxin testing, typically stool PCR or equivalent microbiologic testing, is needed to exclude STEC-HUS.
Coagulation studies help distinguish or identify coexisting DIC, but DIC does not exclude superimposed TMA.
Basic complement tests such as C3 and C4 may be normal and should not be used to rule out CM-HUS.
Extended complement evaluation may include alternative pathway functional testing, complement factor assays, and anti-factor H antibodies.
Genetic testing for complement abnormalities can inform relapse risk and long-term treatment planning, but negative testing does not exclude CM-HUS.
Kidney biopsy may support diagnosis when platelet count and bleeding risk allow; findings may show TMA, fibrin thrombi, ischemic glomerular injury, and acute tubular necrosis.
Direct antiglobulin testing may be misleading in complex in-hospital settings such as drug exposure or transfusion; discordant hemolysis findings warrant reassessment.
Microbiologic evaluation for infectious triggers, including blood cultures, is important in suspected infection-associated CM-HUS.
Interpret complement testing carefully if plasma exchange or complement inhibitors have already been started, as treatment can alter results.

outline.description: Provide a structured differential for MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and AKI, with emphasis on differentiating CM-HUS from other thrombotic microangiopathies and sepsis-related disorders.
key_points: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: suggested by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, often with more prominent neurologic findings and less severe renal injury than HUS.
STEC-HUS: supported by diarrheal prodrome and positive Shiga toxin testing.
Sepsis-associated DIC: characterized by consumptive coagulopathy, prolonged clotting studies, low fibrinogen, bleeding, and microthrombi, though overlap with TMA may occur.
Secondary TMA due to severe infection, autoimmune disease, pregnancy/postpartum states, malignant hypertension, transplantation, or medications.
Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia or drug-induced TMA.
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia: DAT positivity may suggest this, but schistocytosis and renal TMA point elsewhere.
Acute cortical necrosis or ischemic acute tubular necrosis without systemic TMA.
Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome in the appropriate clinical context.
Bone marrow disorders or hemophagocytic syndromes when cytopenias and systemic inflammation predominate.
Acute leukemia or marrow failure syndromes when pancytopenia is present initially.

outline.description: Describe acute stabilization, treatment of the trigger, empiric management while the diagnosis is being clarified, and definitive therapy with complement inhibition. Address special considerations when active infection is present.
key_points: Immediate management includes stabilization, treatment of the precipitating infection, transfusion support as needed, and renal replacement therapy for severe AKI or anuria.
Antibiotic therapy should be directed at the identified or suspected trigger; in Capnocytophaga infection, prompt antimicrobial treatment is essential.
Manage sepsis and DIC supportively while continuing to reassess for evolving TMA.
Because TTP is a medical emergency, plasma exchange is often started empirically when TMA is suspected and ADAMTS13 results are pending.
In CM-HUS, plasma exchange may provide temporary benefit but is not definitive therapy unless an antibody-mediated mechanism is identified.
Eculizumab is the standard targeted therapy for CM-HUS and should be initiated promptly once TTP and STEC-HUS are reasonably excluded and CM-HUS is suspected.
Early complement blockade improves hematologic remission and renal outcomes.
Before eculizumab, administer meningococcal vaccination when feasible; if urgent treatment is required, do not delay life-saving therapy and provide antimicrobial prophylaxis.
Counsel regarding increased susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria during terminal complement blockade.
In infection-triggered cases, timing of eculizumab requires balancing ongoing infectious risk against the risk of irreversible TMA-related organ injury.
Dialysis may be required temporarily or longer term depending on renal recovery.
Monitor hemoglobin, platelet count, LDH, haptoglobin, urine output, and renal function to assess treatment response.
Duration of complement inhibitor therapy should be individualized based on severity, renal recovery, relapse risk, and presence or absence of pathogenic complement abnormalities.
Long-term nephrology follow-up is indicated after the acute episode.

outline.description: Discuss expected outcomes, factors associated with renal and hematologic recovery, and implications of trigger-associated versus hereditary disease. Keep the discussion qualitative and tied to the case-derived themes.
key_points: Hematologic remission is often achievable with effective complement blockade.
Renal recovery is variable and may be incomplete, especially after delayed diagnosis, severe AKI, or dialysis dependence.
Earlier initiation of eculizumab is associated with better kidney outcomes.
Patients may recover urine output and discontinue dialysis yet remain with chronic kidney impairment.
Risk of relapse is influenced by ongoing triggers and underlying complement abnormalities, if present.
Negative genetic testing may suggest lower inherited risk but does not eliminate the possibility of future recurrence.
Careful post-treatment monitoring is required when considering discontinuation of complement inhibition.
Prognosis is also affected by severity of the precipitating infection and extent of multiorgan involvement.

outline.description: Review acute and chronic complications of CM-HUS itself, the precipitating infection, renal failure, and treatment-related issues.
key_points: Severe AKI, anuria, and need for dialysis.
Chronic kidney disease and potential progression to kidney failure.
Persistent or recurrent hemolysis and thrombocytopenia.
Hypertension and long-term renal sequelae after apparent recovery.
Extrarenal ischemic complications, including skin or digital ischemia from microvascular thrombosis.
Complications related to sepsis and DIC, including bleeding, shock, and multiorgan dysfunction.
Transfusion-related complications in heavily supported patients.
Risks associated with plasma exchange, including line infection, bleeding, and allergic reactions.
Increased susceptibility to meningococcal and other encapsulated bacterial infections during eculizumab therapy.
Diagnostic delay when early features are attributed solely to sepsis or DIC.

outline.description: Provide concise, practice-oriented takeaways emphasizing recognition, diagnosis, and management of CM-HUS in complex presentations such as post-infectious sepsis.
key_points: In adults with AKI, thrombocytopenia, and hemolysis, always think in terms of thrombotic microangiopathy until proven otherwise.
Sepsis and DIC do not exclude CM-HUS; a second process may emerge as infection improves.
A sudden isolated hemoglobin drop with rising LDH, low haptoglobin, and schistocytes is a major clue to superimposed TMA.
Normal C3 and C4 levels do not rule out CM-HUS.
ADAMTS13 activity is central for excluding TTP; severe deficiency is the key diagnostic discriminator.
Negative Shiga toxin testing helps move away from STEC-HUS in the right clinical context.
Kidney biopsy can be highly informative when diagnosis remains uncertain and bleeding risk is acceptable.
Capnocytophaga canimorsus should be considered after dog or cat exposure, even in immunocompetent adults.
Eculizumab should not be unduly delayed once CM-HUS is strongly suspected and major alternatives are excluded.
Vaccination, antimicrobial prophylaxis, and close infection surveillance are essential whenever complement blockade is used.
